item.title: 如何尋找歐洲 PhD 職缺：我使用過的網站與資訊管道
item.dc:creator: Tzu-Yao Lin
item.description:
歐洲沒有統一的 PhD 招生方式。有些博士生職位會像一般工作一樣公開招聘，附有研究主題、聘僱期間與薪資；有些則要先找到指導教授，再申請博士班或研究經費。因此，只依賴一個網站通常不夠。

這篇文章整理我在尋找歐洲 PhD 與研究職缺時使用或留意過的資訊管道。它不是完整的申請攻略，而是一份可以開始動手搜尋的資源清單。

專業學會與郵件論壇

如果已經知道自己感興趣的研究領域，可以先加入相關學會或 mailing list。舉例來說，我對數理心理學、統計和心理計量等領域感興趣，因此會加入相關的 mailing lists，持續留意職缺與學術活動資訊：

  • ALLSTAT：以統計學相關資訊為主，除了研討會、課程與學術活動，有時也會出現 PhD、postdoc 或其他研究職缺。
  • MathPsych mailing lists：由 Society for Mathematical Psychology 維護，適合關注數理心理學、認知建模、心理計量與量化心理學的讀者。

我會把 mailing lists 當成補充來源。它們刊登的職缺數量不一定很多，但收到的消息通常比較接近自己的研究領域，也可能比大型職缺平台更早出現在特定研究社群中。

跨國研究職缺平台

EURAXESS

EURAXESS Jobs 是我會優先查看的平台之一。它收錄歐洲各國的研究職缺、funding opportunities 與 hosting offers，也可以依國家、研究領域和職涯階段篩選。

如果想找博士生職位，可以嘗試搜尋：

  • PhD position
  • doctoral researcher
  • doctoral candidate
  • predoctoral researcher
  • 自己的研究領域，例如 psychometrics、quantitative psychology 或 statistics

部分 Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Networks 的博士生職缺也會刊登在 EURAXESS。搜尋時可以加入 MSCA 或 Doctoral Network。

Academic Positions

Academic Positions 收錄不同國家的 PhD、postdoc、researcher 和 faculty positions，可以按照職位類型、國家與研究領域篩選，也能設定 job alert。

這個網站適合用來快速了解目前哪些國家或大學正在招聘，但看到有興趣的職缺後，我仍會回到大學或研究機構的官方網站確認資訊。

FindAPhD

FindAPhD 可以按照學科、國家、研究計畫或指導教授搜尋博士機會。英國的項目尤其多，但也會收錄其他歐洲國家的 PhD projects、programmes 與 funding information。

使用時要注意，不同結果可能代表不同形式的機會。有些是已經有經費的研究計畫，有些是博士課程介紹，也有些需要申請者另外尋找 funding。

各國常用平台

不同國家的招聘方式不完全相同。確定想去的國家後，可以再加入當地常用的平台。

荷蘭

AcademicTransfer 是尋找荷蘭研究職缺的重要平台。荷蘭大學、研究機構與大學醫院會在這裡刊登 PhD、postdoc 和其他學術職位，也可以建立帳號並儲存搜尋條件。

我會先選擇 PhD 類型，再加入自己的方法或研究主題，例如：

  • psychology
  • psychometrics
  • measurement
  • research methodology
  • statistics
  • longitudinal data

關鍵字不宜設得太窄。同一類研究可能使用不同名稱，例如 quantitative psychology、behavioural science 或 data science。

比利時

比利時的 PhD 職缺可以先從 EURAXESS 和 Academic Positions 開始搜尋。不過，這些跨國平台上的資料取決於招聘單位是否另外刊登，因此不一定涵蓋各大學的所有職缺。比較保險的做法，是把跨國平台當成發現職缺的入口，再定期查看感興趣大學的官方招聘頁面。這不是說跨國平台不可靠，而是不能假設它們一定完整。

以下是幾所比利時大學的官方職缺頁：

  • KU Leuven Jobsite：可以查看 PhD、academic staff 和其他校內職缺，也能設定 job alerts。
  • Ghent University Jobs：包含 PhD students、doctoral fellows、researchers 和其他學術職位。Ghent University 也提到，申請 PhD 除了回應公開職缺，也可能透過聯絡特定教授開始。
  • UHasselt Vacancies：可以依 academic staff、research staff 與 PhD scholarships 等類別查看職缺。
  • University of Antwerp Vacancies：包含 academic staff、research groups 與合作機構的職缺；英文頁面也提醒，完整名單有時需要一併查看荷蘭文頁面。
  • VUB Jobs：可以查看 Vrije Universiteit Brussel 的 PhD、researcher 和 academic personnel 職缺。

如果已經鎖定特定研究團隊，我還會查看該團隊或系所的消息頁面。部分職缺可能先由研究團隊、教授或學術社群分享，之後才出現在大學的中央招聘系統。

法國

Research in France 由 Campus France 維護，可以搜尋 doctoral programmes、博士研究題目、funding 與 doctoral schools。

法國的職缺或博士題目可能區分為已有經費的職位，以及需要申請者自行取得獎學金的題目。閱讀公告時，要特別確認 funding 欄位與申請方式。

英國

英國的博士計畫可以從 FindAPhD 開始，再到各大學的 postgraduate research 或 jobs 頁面確認。

搜尋結果中可能同時包含 funded studentships 和需要自費或另外申請獎學金的 programmes，因此不能只看研究主題，也要確認 tuition fees、stipend 和國際學生資格。

挪威

Jobbnorge 是挪威常見的招聘平台之一，除了其他公共部門職缺，也能找到大學與研究機構刊登的 PhD positions。

部分公告的標題或頁面可能以挪威文顯示，可以直接使用職位名稱、學校名稱或 PhD 搜尋。

直接查看大學與研究團隊

大型平台很方便，但不一定會涵蓋所有機會。我通常也會整理一份自己感興趣的大學、研究中心和研究團隊清單，定期查看它們的官方 jobs 或 vacancies 頁面。

如果在其他網站或社群媒體看到職缺轉貼，我會再回到招聘機構的官方頁面確認：

  • 申請截止日期；
  • 職位是 employment contract、studentship 還是 scholarship；
  • 研究主題與指導團隊；
  • 學歷、方法能力與語言要求；
  • 需要提交哪些申請文件；
  • 預計開始日期。

平台上的職缺可以當成線索，實際申請仍應以招聘單位的官方公告為準。

社群媒體與研究社群

教授、研究團隊與學會有時會在 LinkedIn、X/Twitter 或其他學術社群分享新職缺。若已經知道自己感興趣的領域，可以追蹤：

  • 相關研究者與實驗室；
  • 專業學會；
  • doctoral schools；
  • 大型研究計畫；
  • 歐洲研究網絡。

社群媒體適合提早發現消息，但貼文可能省略申請資格、截止日期，或在職缺關閉後仍持續流傳。找到有興趣的資訊後，仍應回到招聘單位的官方公告確認。

我的搜尋方式

如果剛開始尋找歐洲 PhD，我會採取以下順序：

  1. 先用 EURAXESS、Academic Positions 和 FindAPhD 了解目前有哪些機會。
  2. 確定優先國家後，加入當地平台，例如荷蘭的 AcademicTransfer。
  3. 訂閱與研究領域相關的 mailing lists。
  4. 整理感興趣的大學與研究團隊，定期查看官方招聘頁面。
  5. 設定 job alerts，但每週仍主動搜尋一次，避免關鍵字設定過窄而漏掉職缺。
  6. 找到合適的機會後，回到招聘單位的官方頁面確認所有條件。

搜尋博士職缺需要一些時間，尤其是研究主題較專門時，不一定每週都會出現完全符合的結果。比起只使用一組關鍵字，我認為同時搜尋研究主題、統計方法和不同職稱會比較實際。

註釋關於這份清單

這是我使用或留意過的資源，不是完整的歐洲 PhD 職缺資料庫。平台功能、網址和招聘方式可能改變；實際申請前，請以大學或研究機構的官方公告為準。

本文連結最後檢查日期：2026-08-30。

item.title: Analysis Notes for a Study of Vaccine Sentiment among Brazilian Healthcare Workers
item.dc:creator: Tzu-Yao Lin
item.description:
NoteAbout this analysis record

This page documents exploratory analyses conducted during the preparation of a collaborative study of vaccine sentiment among Brazilian healthcare workers. It is retained as a public record of the analytical workflow and is not intended as a complete tutorial or as the definitive report of the study.

The final methods, results, and interpretations are reported in Lo et al. (2025), The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on vaccine sentiment among Brazilian healthcare workers: A cross-sectional online survey study.

This page focuses on two parts of the analytical workflow:

  1. Exploring whether the factor structure of 17 vaccine-attitude items could be interpreted in relation to the 5C model of vaccine hesitancy.
  2. Fitting logistic regression models that used the resulting factor scores and other covariates to examine associations with five vaccine-sentiment outcomes.

The page does not document every analysis reported in the published article. Some sections preserve intermediate model comparisons and working decisions made during manuscript development.

1 Data availability and privacy

The participant-level dataset is restricted and is not distributed with this website. The original working file contained direct or highly identifying fields, including network identifiers, precise timestamps, unique response identifiers, and free-text responses. Even after excluding those fields, combinations of demographic, professional, health, and attitude variables may still allow individuals to be singled out or linked to other information.

The code and frozen aggregate outputs are retained to document the analytical workflow. Authorised researchers must store the dataset outside the repository and supply its path through BRAZIL_DATA_PATH; the analysis rejects paths inside the website project. Public outputs should contain aggregate statistics and model results rather than participant-level records. Consequently, this page supports transparency about the analysis process but is not a fully executable public reproduction package.

2 Data preparation

First, the necessary R packages are loaded.

Code 
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(haven) # for reading STATA dta files
library(psych) # for factor analysis
library(GPArotation)
library(corrplot) # for correlation plots
library(gt)

# Make randomized factor-rotation starts reproducible across renders.
set.seed(20250328)

The analysis uses a restricted participant-level dataset that is stored separately from this public repository. Authorised researchers can supply its external file path through the BRAZIL_DATA_PATH environment variable.

Code 
data_path <- Sys.getenv("BRAZIL_DATA_PATH")

if (!nzchar(data_path)) {
  stop("Set BRAZIL_DATA_PATH to the restricted dataset outside this project.")
}

data_path <- normalizePath(data_path, mustWork = TRUE)
project_dir <- Sys.getenv(
  "QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR",
  unset = normalizePath("../../..", mustWork = TRUE)
)
project_dir <- normalizePath(project_dir, mustWork = TRUE)

if (
  identical(data_path, project_dir) ||
    startsWith(data_path, paste0(project_dir, .Platform$file.sep))
) {
  stop("BRAZIL_DATA_PATH must point outside the public website project.")
}

rawdata <- read_dta(data_path) |>
  select(
    gender, age_class, member, edu, prof, w_setting, chronic,
    matches("vac_gen_\\d"),
    covid_pro_1:covid_oblig_2,
    covid_leaders:covid_earlyaccess,
    cov_pro_3, change_vac_1, change_vac_2, change_vac_3,
    change_HealthSy_1, fear, knowledge
  )

Only variables required by the analyses below are retained in memory. Direct identifiers, network identifiers, precise timestamps, and free-text responses are excluded.

Key observations from the data preparation include:

  • Missing values are present, denoted by NA for numeric variables and empty strings (““) for character variables.
  • Many variables have the class haven_labelled. These labelled variables require careful handling and appropriate transformation before analysis.

Next, the variables relevant to this analysis are selected.

Code 
data <- rawdata |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(., "")))

3 Vaccine hesitancy (VH)

3.1 Prepare variables

Before conducting the factor analysis, 17 variables related to general vaccine attitudes and specific COVID-19 attitudes were selected.

  drop_na()

This non-sequential coding implies an assumption that the interval between ‘Disagree’ (2) and ‘Agree’ (4) is twice that of the other adjacent intervals. Treating these data as interval scale in the analysis relies on this assumption.

The Pearson correlations and maximum-likelihood factor models below therefore treat the recoded four-point responses as approximately continuous.

Before performing the factor analysis, a correlation matrix is examined to visually inspect potential clustering among the attitude variables.

Code 
cor_mat <- cor(fa_data)

# Copy from https://www.sthda.com/english/wiki/visualize-correlation-matrix-using-correlogram

cor.mtest <- function(mat, ...) {
    mat <- as.matrix(mat)
    n <- ncol(mat)
    p.mat<- matrix(NA, n, n)
    diag(p.mat) <- 0
    for (i in 1:(n - 1)) {
        for (j in (i + 1):n) {
            tmp <- cor.test(mat[, i], mat[, j], ...)
            p.mat[i, j] <- p.mat[j, i] <- tmp$p.value
        }
    }
  colnames(p.mat) <- rownames(p.mat) <- colnames(mat)
  p.mat
}
# matrix of the p-value of the correlation
p.mat <- cor.mtest(cor_mat)

corrplot(
  cor_mat, method="color", type="upper", order="hclust", 
  addCoef.col = "black", # Add coefficient of correlation
  tl.col="black", tl.srt=45, tl.cex=0.6, #Text label color and rotation
  cl.cex = 0.5, number.cex = 0.75,
  # Combine with significance
  p.mat = p.mat, sig.level = 0.01, insig = "blank", 
  # hide correlation coefficient on the principal diagonal
  diag=FALSE
)
CautionAudit note: significance masking in the correlation plot

In this recorded workflow, cor.mtest() was applied to cor_mat rather than to the original item-level data. The significance masking in the displayed correlation plot should therefore be treated as an exploratory display rather than as a valid set of tests for the original item correlations. The correlation matrix itself and the downstream factor analyses do not depend on p.mat.

The correlation matrix suggests potential clustering into two or three groups:

  1. vac_gen_4, covid_ag_1, covid_ag_2, and covid_over18 form a cluster.
  2. Other variables (except for vac_gen_6) form a cluster.
  3. vac_gen_6 might form its own cluster but appears closer to the second cluster. Subsequent analyses did not identify a distinct factor defined by this item.

Note that this is a preliminary observation based on correlations. The underlying latent structure will be formally investigated using factor analysis.

3.2 Factor analysis

3.2.1 Pre-tests and scree plots

Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure and Bartlett’s test of sphericity are used to assess the suitability of the data for factor analysis.

NoteInterpretation notes: factorability diagnostics
  • The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) statistic summarizes whether the pattern of correlations is sufficiently compact for common-factor analysis; larger values indicate greater factorability.
  • Bartlett’s test evaluates whether the correlation matrix differs from an identity matrix. A small p-value indicates that the items are not mutually uncorrelated, but it does not determine the number of factors or establish that a particular factor solution is appropriate.
Code 
# Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin statistic
KMO_result <- KMO(cor_mat)
print(KMO_result)

The recorded KMO value and Bartlett test were used at the time as preliminary checks of factorability. These diagnostics do not, by themselves, establish an appropriate dimensional model.

CautionAudit note: sample size in Bartlett’s test

The recorded call supplied nrow(data) as the sample size, whereas cor_mat was calculated from the complete-case dataset fa_data. The frozen chi-square statistic is retained here as part of the original workflow, but a reanalysis should use the effective sample size corresponding to the correlation matrix. This issue does not alter the subsequent factor-model estimates, which were fitted directly to fa_data.

A key challenge in EFA is determining the optimal number of factors to retain. Parallel analysis is employed to guide the decision on the number of factors. This procedure compares the eigenvalues from the actual data’s correlation matrix with eigenvalues derived from random data matrices of the same size. The number of factors suggested is the count of actual eigenvalues that exceed the corresponding eigenvalues (or the 95th percentile thereof) from the random data.

Code 
fa.parallel(fa_data, fm = "ml", fa = "fa", nfactors = 1) 
Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  3  and the number of components =  NA

With maximum-likelihood factor analysis specified (fm = "ml"), the displayed parallel analysis suggested retaining three factors. This result was treated as one input to the exploratory comparison rather than as a definitive decision. Visual inspection of the scree plot could support a smaller solution, while the Kaiser eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule suggested one factor; the latter was not used as the primary retention criterion.

This analysis does not aim to develop a new measurement instrument or uncover ‘true’ latent constructs. Instead, the goal is to explore whether the factor structure in this data aligns with the established 5C model. To facilitate comparison with the 5C model, solutions with 3, 4, and 5 factors will be examined. Therefore, 3-, 4-, and 5-factor models are explored below. For each number of factors (3, 4, and 5), both orthogonal (“Varimax”) and oblique (“Oblimin”) rotations are applied. Factor scores are estimated using the regression method.

NoteInterpretation notes: factor solutions
  • Factor loadings describe the relation between each item and the factors.
  • h2 is the communality, or the proportion of an item’s variance represented by the retained factors; u2 is its uniqueness (1 - h2).
  • com is Hofmann’s item-complexity index. Values near one indicate that an item is primarily associated with one factor, whereas larger values indicate more complex loading patterns.
  • Model comparison also considered cross-loadings, factor correlations, simple structure, theoretical interpretability, and the proportion of variance represented. Conventional numerical cutoffs were treated as descriptive guides rather than universal decision rules.

NoteInterpretation notes: model fit
  • The likelihood-ratio chi-square evaluates exact fit and is sensitive to sample size.
  • RMS and cRMS summarize residual discrepancies between the observed and model-implied correlations.
  • RMSEA assesses approximate fit and should be interpreted with its uncertainty interval when available.
  • TLI compares the proposed model with a more restrictive baseline model while penalizing complexity.
  • BIC balances fit and complexity; lower values favor a model within the set being compared.

3.2.5 Working decision at this stage

The recorded fit indices did not point uniformly to a single solution. The displayed parallel analysis suggested three factors, whereas BIC was lower for the four-factor solutions. The five-factor solutions showed more favorable TLI and RMSEA values than the smaller solutions.

At this stage of manuscript development, the five-factor oblique solution (fa5_ob) was retained as the working model. The decision considered the study’s connection to the 5C framework, the interpretability of the loading pattern, correlations among the factors, and the model-fit indices. It should not be read as evidence that the statistical criteria independently established a five-factor structure.

EFA was used because the original questionnaire was not designed a priori as a direct operationalization of the 5C constructs. The analysis therefore explored the underlying loading structure before interpreting its relation to the 5C framework.

4 Vaccine sentiment (VS)

The working analysis used the following five sentiment variables:

  1. change_vac_1 (S1): My attitude towards vaccination (in general) has not been influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic.
  2. change_vac_2 (S2): The COVID-19 pandemic has increased my confidence in the safety of vaccines.
  3. change_HealthSy_1 (S3): The COVID-19 pandemic has increased my confidence in the health system of my country.
  4. change_vac_3 (S4): From now on, I will pay more attention to updating my vaccination schedule in general.
  5. cov_pro_3 (S5): I am keen to receive another COVID-19 vaccination if the health authority recommends it.

The S1-S5 labels preserve the ordering used in this working analysis record. They do not correspond numerically to the VS1-VS5 labels in the published article:

Each item was treated as a binary outcome (agree/strongly agree versus disagree/strongly disagree). The staged logistic regression models recorded during manuscript development are summarized in Table Table 4.

NoteScope of this section

The models below preserve the sequence in which demographic, occupational, fear, knowledge, and factor-score predictors were added during the working analysis. They do not document every model, diagnostic, or sensitivity analysis reported in the published article. The article and its supplementary materials remain the definitive source for the final estimates and interpretations.

4.1 Define variables

Code

demography_var <- c("gender", "age_class", "edu", "chronic")
working_var <- c("member", "prof", "w_setting")
fn_var <- c("fear", "knowledge")

  drop_na(all_of(attitude_var)) |> 
  select(
    all_of(sentiment_var), 
    all_of(demography_var), 
    all_of(working_var),
    all_of(fn_var),
    all_of(attitude_var)) |> 
  add_column(fa_scores)

The variables were coded as follows:

  • Outcomes: S1-S5 were recoded as binary factors (0 = disagree/strongly disagree; 1 = agree/strongly agree).
  • Gender (gender): female or male; “I prefer not to answer” was treated as missing.
  • Age group (age_class): <35, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, or 75+.
  • Education (edu): medical degree or other; the latter combined the remaining education categories.
  • Chronic disease (chronic): yes or no; “I prefer not to answer” was treated as missing.
  • Association membership (member): yes or no; “I don’t know” was treated as missing.
  • Profession (prof): nutrition, pharmacy, physician, or other.
  • Work setting (w_setting): community, hospital, private, university, or other.

  mutate(

    # Demographic variables

    age_class = as_factor(age_class),

4.2 Logistic regression models

4.2.1 Sentiment 1 (S1)

The formulas for the five staged models for Sentiment 1 (change_vac_1) are defined as follows:

m2_str <- str_c(m1_str, " + ", str_flatten(working_var, " + "))
m3_str <- str_c(m2_str, " + ", "fear")

Each model was estimated using logistic regression with a binomial family and logit link.

Code

                 ~ glm(as.formula(.), family = binomial, lr_data))

The working odds-ratio estimates for S1 are recorded in Table Table 5.

Code 
extract_esti <- function(lr) {
  coef <- summary(lr)$coefficients
  var_name <- rownames(coef)
  esti <- coef[, 1]
  OR <- exp(esti) |> round(2)
  se <- coef[, 2]
  p_value <- coef[, 4]
  conf_l <- exp(esti - qnorm(1-0.05/2) * se) |> round(2)
  conf_u <- exp(esti + qnorm(1-0.05/2) * se) |> round(2)
  p_sig <- cut(p_value, 
               breaks = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 1),
               labels = c("*** ", "**  ", "*   ", "    ", "    "),
               include.lowest = TRUE)
  result <- str_glue("{format(OR)}{p_sig}<br>[{format(conf_l)}, {format(conf_u)}]")
  tibble(vars = var_name, esti = result)
}

item.dc:creator: Tzu-Yao Lin
item.description:
NoteAbout this analysis record

This page documents analyses conducted during the preparation of a collaborative study of coffee consumption, polygenic risk score, and diabetes using data from The Maastricht Study. It is retained as a public record of the analytical workflow and is not intended as a complete tutorial or as the definitive report of the study.

The final methods, results, and interpretations are reported in Rao et al. (2025), Interaction between coffee consumption and polygenic risk score in relation to diabetes: insights from the Maastricht study.

1 Purpose and analytical scope

This record arose while checking and developing the statistical analyses for a collaborative cross-sectional study using data from The Maastricht Study. The outcome distinguished participants with normal glucose metabolism (NGM), prediabetes, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The main exposures were habitual coffee consumption and a polygenic risk score (PRS) for T2DM.

The scientific questions were whether coffee consumption and PRS were separately associated with the prevalence of prediabetes and T2DM, and whether the association between PRS and glucose-metabolism status differed across levels of coffee consumption. Because these analyses use cross-sectional observational data, the estimates describe associations with prevalent glucose-metabolism categories; they do not by themselves establish causal or preventive effects.

1.1 Questions documented in this record

The working analysis focused on five practical questions that arose during manuscript preparation:

  1. How should missing observations be handled so that candidate models are fitted to comparable data?
  2. Is an ordinal logistic model appropriate for the three glucose-metabolism categories?
  3. If the proportional-odds assumption is not tenable, should the outcome be analyzed using two binary logistic regressions or one multinomial logistic regression?
  4. How do estimates for coffee consumption and PRS change across the proposed covariate sets?
  5. How should the coffee-by-PRS interaction and odds ratios for joint exposure categories be evaluated and presented?

This page concentrates on these model-development questions and the construction of working result tables. It does not document every analysis reported in the published article. In particular, the published study also reports dose-response and sensitivity analyses that are outside the scope of this record. Some sections below preserve working questions, intermediate comparisons, and decisions that differ from the final publication.

2 Data availability and privacy

The participant-level dataset used for this analysis is restricted and is not distributed with this public website repository. The file contains individual-level health, demographic, behavioral, medication, socioeconomic, and polygenic-risk variables. Whether any subset may be shared depends on the original consent, data-use agreement, ethics approval, and applicable institutional requirements; repository publication should not be assumed to be permitted.

For local reproduction by an authorized researcher, the dataset must be stored outside the repository and supplied through the CDP_DATA_PATH environment variable. The analysis rejects paths inside the website project. Public outputs should contain aggregate summaries and model results rather than participant-level records.

WarningWorking decision: complete-case dataset

At this stage of the analysis, the treatment of missing observations in the source preprocessing was not fully documented. For the model comparisons below, I constructed one complete-case dataset by excluding any participant with NA, -999, or -888 on at least one of the 20 selected variables.

Using a common analysis sample ensured that differences in AIC or likelihood-ratio tests across the candidate models were not caused by fitting the models to different sets of participants. This produced a working sample of 6,224 complete cases after excluding 1,444 rows. By comparison, the published article reports an included study sample of 7,668 and labels its main association table as . This record does not establish how the difference between that reporting and the complete-case workflow shown here was resolved.

Complete-case analysis was a working decision for comparability, not a general recommendation that it is optimal. The substantial missingness in Step_wake may affect precision and the population represented by the fitted models, and this page does not include a missing-data sensitivity analysis.

ImportantOpen questions recorded during analysis

The following questions were recorded before the manuscript decisions were finalized:

  1. What was the substantive reason for categorizing PRS and coffee consumption into low, medium, and high groups rather than retaining continuous measures? If tertiles were retained, should an additional trend or dose-response analysis be reported?

  2. What interpretive advantage did tertiles provide, and how should their simpler presentation be weighed against the loss of information caused by categorization?

The published study subsequently described both variables as study-population tertiles and additionally examined coffee consumption using a continuous dose-response analysis. The final article should therefore be used for the definitive rationale and specification.

4 Model development record

4.1 Outcome-model choice

get_OR_CI <- function(multi_model, DV_level, EV_level, alpha = 0.05) {
  esti <- coef(multi_model)[DV_level, , drop = FALSE]
  .cov_mat <- vcov(multi_model)
  .select_variable <- str_detect(colnames(.cov_mat), DV_level)
  cov_mat <- .cov_mat[.select_variable, .select_variable]
  
  cont <- matrix(multi_model$coefnames %in% EV_level, nrow = 1)
  l <- cont %*% t(esti)
  OR <- exp(l) |> round(2)
  SE <- sqrt(cont %*% cov_mat %*% t(cont))
  lower_CI <- exp(l - qnorm(1-alpha/2) * SE) |> round(2)
  upper_CI <- exp(l + qnorm(1-alpha/2) * SE) |> round(2)
  
  str_glue("{OR} <br> ({lower_CI}, {upper_CI})")
}

For the candidate models shown above, the likelihood-ratio tests did not provide evidence that adding the categorical coffee-by-PRS interaction terms improved model fit. The corresponding main-effects models (prs_cof1, prs_cof2, and prs_cof3) were therefore retained for the working association tables. 5 Relation to the published article

This page preserves a subset of the analyses and decisions considered during manuscript preparation. It is an analytical record rather than a reconstruction of every final analysis, and the published article is the definitive source for the study methods, results, and interpretation.

Several features of the final analysis are important when reading this record:

  1. The published article reports an included sample of 7,668 and labels its main association table as , whereas the complete-case working models on this page use 6,224 participants. The available record does not reconcile this difference.
  2. The final article used multinomial logistic regression with NGM as the reference outcome and reported three sequential covariate-adjustment sets.
  3. Education was included in Model 1 of the published analysis. By contrast, the working candidate formulas preserved above add Education in the third covariate set.
  4. The final categorical coffee-by-PRS interaction was evaluated in the fully adjusted model using a likelihood-ratio test. The reported value was .21, providing no evidence of multiplicative interaction in that analysis.
  5. The published work additionally examined coffee consumption using restricted cubic splines and conducted sensitivity analyses focused on newly diagnosed diabetes and recruitment period. Those analyses are not reproduced on this page.

In the final results, medium and high coffee-consumption categories were associated with lower odds of prevalent prediabetes and T2DM, whereas higher PRS categories were associated with higher odds. The dose-response analysis suggested a potentially U-shaped association between coffee consumption and both outcomes. These cross-sectional associations should not be interpreted as evidence that coffee consumption causes a reduction in diabetes risk.

For the complete methods, results, sensitivity analyses, and interpretation, see Rao et al. (2025), Interaction between coffee consumption and polygenic risk score in relation to diabetes: insights from the Maastricht study.

Welcome to my blog. I started this space to share updates on my research, notes from what I am reading and learning, and things I discover while working with R, statistics, and psychology. I may also write about personal thoughts and experiences along the way.

Why start a personal blog? The reason is simple: I want to share what I learn instead of keeping it in my own notes.

When you’ve written the same code 3 times, write a function.

When you’ve given the same in-person advice 3 times, write a blog post.

— David Robinson (@drob, November 9, 2017)

I still don’t know exactly what this blog will become, but that is part of the point. I would rather start now and let it take shape over time. Thanks for reading.
